actionRequired.description:
Action required for the custom scheduler plugin developers. 
Here's the breaking change in `EnqueueExtension` in the scheduling framework. 
The `EventsToRegister` in `EnqueueExtension` changed the return value from `ClusterEvent` to `ClusterEventWithHint`. `ClusterEventWithHint` allows each plugin to filter out more useless events via the callback function named `QueueingHintFn`.
When the scheduling queue receives a cluster event, before moving each Pod from unschedulable pod pool to activeQ/backoffQ, it will call QueueingHintFn of plugins that rejected each Pod in the previous scheduling cycle.
Depending on the value returned from QueueingHintFn, the scheduling queue changes how it queues each Pod:
- if more than one QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately, it queues Pod to activeQ.
- If no QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately and more than one plugin returns QueueAfterBackoff, it queues Pod to backoffQ if Pod is backing off, or to activeQ if Pod's backoff has already finished.
- If all QueueingHintFn return QueueSkip, it puts this pod back to the unschedulable pod pool

Having appropriate QueueingHintFn contributes to reducing useless retries and thus improves the overall scheduler's performance.

**How can I migrate?**

For backward compatibility, nil `QueueingHintFn` is treated as always returning QueueAfterBackoff. 
So, if you want to just keep the existing behavior, you can register `ClusterEventWithHint` with no `QueueingHintFn` in it. 
But, registering appropriate `QueueingHintFn` is, of course, better from a scheduling performance perspective.

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

A misconfigured pod with a preStopHook that hangs indefinitely and pod ignoring SIGTERM can result in the pod taking 2X (double) the termination grace period seconds to terminate.
 

### What did you expect to happen?

The time to terminate the pod should always be <= termination grace period seconds including prestop hook execution time as documented in https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#hook-handler-execution

```

  name: prestop-repro

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60

  - name: busybox

issueContext.title: client-go/kubectl rejects discovery API responses with charset encoding info
issueContext.body:
We are using `client-go` (and `kubectl`) to interact with Kubernetes clusters behind a couple of proxy layers. One of these proxies completes the `Content-Type` headers to include character encoding details.

This was working fine until recently, when client-go/kubectl have started to fail when interacting with the discovery API. It seems that a recent change has made kubectl more restrictive of the content-type that it expects. I suspect that it is related to this commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773

For example, this is an error from a kubectl command:
```
...
E0422 16:28:02.626222   86629 memcache.go:265] couldn't get current server API group list: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626258   86629 cached_discovery.go:120] skipped caching discovery info due to Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626346   86629 shortcut.go:100] Error loading discovery information: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
```

We can of course try to fix it on our end, removing that charset information. However, it is a valid content-type and the way kubectl is handling the content-type there seems like it is relying on implementation details of kube-apiserver (that it does not add metadata to the content-type). I propose to fix this issue in `kubectl`, by properly parsing and handling the content-type.

issueContext.title: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L424)

bugOrRegression.author: marseel

issueContext.title: Improve exponential backoff in reflector
issueContext.body:
Currently, reflector uses two backoff managers: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/2a5f18df73b70cb85c26a3785b06162f3d513cf5/tools/cache/reflector.go#L223
One is used for initial list call and other for watch call. 

Imagine following scenaraion when k8s apiserver is under very heavy load:
1. At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds (due to APF throtling and receiving `429`)
2. Reflector tries to run `Watch` request and uses separate backoffManager - so again spams k8s apiserver with `Watch` requests
3. If Watch does not succeed during Etcd compaction window (2.5 - 5 minutes usually) at some point it will receive `resourceVersionTooOld` and go back to point 1, spamming k8s apiserver again with List calls (because first backoffManager for List got reseted after 2 minutes of retries for Watch requests)

I propose we combine these two backoff managers into one. 
If we combine these two backoffManagers into one, it will work like this:
- At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (still with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds
- Tries to make first watch call instantly (as there is no backoff on this path)
- If it fails, it will makre retries every (30, 60)s
- If watch request fails all the times during Etcd compaction window it will go back to List call, but already being throttled with (30, 60)s window. 

/sig scalability

issueContext.title: Indexed Jobs can break with high number of parallelism or completions
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Currently, the maximum number of completions is MAX_INT32, around 2e9 and the maximum parallelism is 1e5.

When using these values, and assuming a very unlucky case, the field `.status.completedIndexes` can fill up the maximum size for objects in etcd (around 1.5Mi)

/sig apps
/sig scalability

### What did you expect to happen?

An Indexed Job with the maximum number of completions and parallelism to be correctly tracked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sample-job
spec:
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 2000000000
  parallelism: 100000
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: bad
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import os
          import time
          id = int(os.environ.get("JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"))
          if id > 1000000000 and id % 3 == 0:
            time.sleep(10000)
      restartPolicy: Never
```

In other words, every index multiple of 3 takes too long to terminate.

### Anything else we need to know?

In the example above, the number of characters needed by the `completedIndexes` field is:

`(10+1)*2*1e5`, roughly 2Mi, where:
- 10 is the number of characters for a number
- 1 for the separating character.
- 2 for the consecutive numbers
- 1e5 for the number of "holes" in the `completedIndexes`, based on the parallelism.

### Kubernetes version

1.21 and newer (when IndexedJob was introduced)

issueContext.title: meaning of sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total given MinimizeIPTablesRestore
issueContext.body:
The `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total` metric is defined as "Number of proxy iptables rules programmed".

In the past, that effectively meant "the total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns". But post-`MinimizeIPTablesRestore`, it now ends up being "the number of iptables rules that changed in the last sync". (FWIW this is only a change for the `nat` half of the metric; currently we always rewrite all `filter` rules, even in a partial sync, so the `filter` half of the metric is still "correct".)

There are arguments for either meaning, but I think the traditional ("total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns") is more useful?

One possibility would be to only set the metric during full syncs, but in that case we might go a very long time without updating it, and it would get out of date.

Another possibility would be that instead of setting that metric from the `iptables-restore` _input_, we could set it from the `iptables-save` _output_. This would mean that it would always lag by (at least) one sync (since it would be set based on the rules we are replacing rather than the rules we are creating) but that would at least be more up-to-date than waiting for the next full resync. (In `largeClusterMode`, it would lag a bit more, only getting updated once every `syncPeriod` (default 30s).)

If we think it's important to have it always be up-to-date then we could try to figure out some way to calculate the right value during a partial update... in that case we'd have to run through the code that currently gets bypassed during a partial update, and have it decide what rules are needed, but not actually try to write them.

/sig network

### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```

```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

issueContext.title: kubectl wait on arbitrary jsonpath with unknown value
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

#83094 describes the `kubectl wait` functionality that allows to wait for a JSONPath expression condition to match a value. For example, the following command waits for a pod with the name `busybox1` reaching "Running" phase:

```bash
kubectl wait pod/busybox1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Running
```

The proposal is to extend the syntax of the command by supporting _any non-empty_ values. The extended syntax will look like the following:

```terminal
jsonpath='{JSONPath expression}'[=value]
```

In the new syntax if the `=value` is provided, the behavior will be, as today, to return when the JSONPath expression matches the value. If `=value` is omitted, the behavior will be to return when the JSONPath expression exists and has _any non-empty_  value.



### Why is this needed?

Unfortunately, the use of current syntax of the JSONPath conditions is limited because it is not always possible to know in advance the value that the JSONPath expression will get. For example, if we would like to wait for a LoadBalancer service with the name `loadbalancer1` to get IP "10.0.0.1", we will run the following command:

```bash
kubectl wait service/loadbalancer1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[].ip}'="10.0.0.1"
```

However, there is no guarantee that the service will get this IP. It can get any other. So, if we want to wait until the LoadBalancer service will get an IP, any IP, we cannot use `kubectl wait` command. Like this, we cannot wait for annotations and labels that are dynamically assigned when their value can vary.

Today DevOps engineers are forced to compose scripts where they implement the waiting logic by calling `kubectl get` in loops (e.g. [this question][1] on Stackoverflow).

[1]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66114851/kubectl-wait-for-service-to-get-external-ip

issueContext.title: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from there on. So basically Kubernetes wouldn't do much in terms of scheduling, but takes over from there.

### What did you expect to happen?

TBH I expected it to fail and it did. The resource claims won't work, since the scheduler plugin isn't getting a chance to do its thing.

Just use DRA with Pod spec nodeName field, one needs a DRA driver obviously.

feature.description:
Action required for the custom scheduler plugin developers. 
Here's the breaking change in `EnqueueExtension` in the scheduling framework. 
The `EventsToRegister` in `EnqueueExtension` changed the return value from `ClusterEvent` to `ClusterEventWithHint`. `ClusterEventWithHint` allows each plugin to filter out more useless events via the callback function named `QueueingHintFn`.
When the scheduling queue receives a cluster event, before moving each Pod from unschedulable pod pool to activeQ/backoffQ, it will call QueueingHintFn of plugins that rejected each Pod in the previous scheduling cycle.
Depending on the value returned from QueueingHintFn, the scheduling queue changes how it queues each Pod:
- if more than one QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately, it queues Pod to activeQ.
- If no QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately and more than one plugin returns QueueAfterBackoff, it queues Pod to backoffQ if Pod is backing off, or to activeQ if Pod's backoff has already finished.
- If all QueueingHintFn return QueueSkip, it puts this pod back to the unschedulable pod pool

Having appropriate QueueingHintFn contributes to reducing useless retries and thus improves the overall scheduler's performance.

**How can I migrate?**

For backward compatibility, nil `QueueingHintFn` is treated as always returning QueueAfterBackoff. 
So, if you want to just keep the existing behavior, you can register `ClusterEventWithHint` with no `QueueingHintFn` in it. 
But, registering appropriate `QueueingHintFn` is, of course, better from a scheduling performance perspective.

issueContext.title: dynamic resource allocation: delete generated ResourceClaims
issueContext.body:
At the moment, dynamic resource allocation relies on the garbage collector to delete a ResourceClaim that was created from a template for a specific pod. But that garbage collection only happens when the pod actually gets deleted.

That means that for pods that linger after having failed or completed (manually created test pods, jobs), resources remain allocated for extended periods of time although they are not needed anymore and could be reused for other claims.

The solution outlined in the KEP is to make the `resourceclaim` controller also responsible for deleting ResourceClaims when it detects that a pod no longer needs the claim.

issueContext.title: DRA: delayed allocation: deallocate after use
issueContext.body:
When a ResourceClaim:
- uses delayed allocation
- does not get created for a specific pod (i.e. not from a template)

then it currently gets allocated and remains allocated until:
- scheduling of a pod fails because the node originally chosen for the allocation isn't suitable, in which case the scheduler triggers deallocation via `claim.status.deallocationRequested`
- the user deletes the claim

What we want instead is that deallocation gets triggered when the last user of such an allocated claim gets removed from `claim.status.reservedFor`. To avoid races, deallocation must be done through `deallocationRequested`.

This can be implemented either as a controller or directly in the API server.

issueContext.title: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197553760-cfd8a8f0-0996-4ee7-8f8c-5ea72e06bf8d.png)
* Remove 99% of the state
* [issue] Observe memory usage (it stays around ~1GB, despite state taking ~10M)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197555163-adff7e50-e0db-4c75-8397-929b08dc9c08.png)
* Recreate the state (with the same name)
* [issue] The memory usage grows to ~2G
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197557325-f3aef1f3-c003-4f17-83db-5aac06ab5643.png)


### Anything else we need to know?

This seems to be consequence of the:
* ConfigMapList using []ConfigMap type (not []*ConfigMap)
* Reflector taking pointer to those objects https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fe9d04763b94366a7a80a1ef3d9f83337eac722e/stag

issueContext.title: [SIG-Node]  Cgroups v2 memory.oom.group support (kill all pids in a pod on oom)
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Follow up on meeting of 28-03-2022 [Meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ne57gvidMEWXR70OxxnRkYquAoMpt56o75oZtg-OeBg/edit#heading=h.2cz4ars29skh) - [Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1679649131585659)

In the meeting was specified that this most likely won't need a KEP and should be started with a Issue

I see that the kernel in cgroups v2 has an option memory.oom.group which would make all the pids of a given container to get killed on OOM:
```
+  memory.oom.group
+	A read-write single value file which exists on non-root
+	cgroups.  The default value is "0".
+
+	Determines whether the cgroup should be treated as a single
+	unit by the OOM killer. If set, the cgroup and its descendants
+	are killed together or not at all. This can be used to avoid
+	partial kills to guarantee workload integrity.
+
+	Tasks with the OOM protection (oom_score_adj set to -1000)
+	are treated as an exception and are never killed.
+
+	If the OOM killer is invoked in a cgroup, it's not going
+	to kill any tasks outside of this cgroup, regardless
+	memory.oom.group values of ancestor cgroups.
```
@mrunalp  @SergeyKanzhelev 

### Why is this needed?

Some workloads that fork the process in the container, when the OOM kicks in, it kills only one process of the cgroup, causing a lot of noise due to process failures but health checks being successfull. We think that for our scenarios, killing all the pids in the containter would be better.

issueContext.title: undeprecate kubelet --provider-id flag
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Un-deperecate the `--provider-id` kubelet flag, as this option is typically set per-node similar to `--node-ip` (which is not deprecated).

Or more generally, consider not deprecating fields available in config that make sense to set per-node.

### Why is this needed?

I noticed this while trying to ensure KIND moves towards not setting any deprecated flags, this one is tricky because it's not a fixed value.
https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kind/pull/2764

For a lot of kubernetes users, kubeadm is used for bootstrapping, and kubeadm supports supplying additional kubelet flags when configuring each node, but the kubelet config is cluster-wide, created during setting up the first node and uploaded to a configmap then used for all nodes.

In the future kubeadm may have the ability to do per-node kubelet config, but that effort will probably be involved and isn't staffed at the moment.

_technically_ you could run kubeadm in phases and then modify the config, but this is more complex to implement.

It's possible this won't be necessary if kubeadm patches can be extended to kubelet which may be a smaller feature change for kubeadm, but personally I think being able to configure simple per-node strings with a flag override is desirable for implementing clusters, and we've had the flag for many years with no trouble ...

 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/issues/1682#issuecomment-1124027039


The actual deprecation seems to be due to a blanket deprecation on things possible to set in config, and not targeted at this flag in particular.

See discussion in https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1652465646070179

issueContext.title: helper function for unused storage feature in pkg/proxy/util
issueContext.body:
`pkg/proxy/util/utils.go` (which is supposed to be utility functions for kube-proxy) contains the function `NewFilteredDialContext` and associated struct `FilteredDialogOptions`, which are not used by kube-proxy and have nothing to do with service proxying. They were added in #91785 as part of a storage-related feature.

However this feature was apparently only ever implemented for two storage backends (scaleio and storageos), both of which have since been removed (#101685, #111620). So the current state is that you can set the associated [options in the kube-controller-manager config v1alpha1 API](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91785/commits/f2e23afcf13fef805ad5341bd7a5625de5982d6c#diff-5ad0cddac612ee34ef81af71efaeae956cc08c468cf20ac2bf719aba980a73a6), and kcm constructs a `proxyutil.FilteredDialogOptions` which then gets passed around the volume controller, but there is no code that ever actually _uses_ that object.

I would like to get this code out of `pkg/proxy/util`, because it doesn't belong there. I was originally going to suggest moving it to `pkg/volume/util` or something, but given that it's essentially unused, maybe we should just revert #91785?

/sig storage

issueContext.body:
/sig apps

The code around Job controller exponential backoff delay has a lot of heritage. The purpose of this issue is to collect and discuss cleanup ideas. It was initiated by the backoff discussion under the KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3967#discussion_r1219690984.

Some fixes initiated by the discussion and small cleanups are already handled by the PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118470.

The source of the issue might be that the “backoff” delay is used in two different contexts:
- Value of the exponential backoff delay is computed based on the number of consecutive failures. It’s main purpose is to throttle pod creation rate when the pods fail: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1415-L1419. 
- Value computed by the number of requeues in the queue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1546-L1564

First, I suggest splitting the naming of these two different backoffs. Let’s use “api error backoff delay” and “pod failure backoff delay”. It would be good if the naming in the code reflected this difference.

Second, the “api error backoff delay” is used in non-obvious places:
- When handling a pod which is transitioning to failed phase: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4c40d749006a8895f6718f2b624a3dbe975988ab/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L321 (seems ok to drop)

bugOrRegression.description: Adds an opt-in mitigation for http/2 DOS vulnerabilities for CVE-2023-44487 and CVE-2023-39325 for the API server when the client is unauthenticated. The mitigation may be enabled by setting the `UnauthenticatedHTTP2DOSMitigation` feature gate to `true` (it is disabled by default). An API server fronted by an L7 load balancer that already mitigates these http/2 attacks may choose not to enable the kube-apiserver mitigation to avoid disrupting load balancer → kube-apiserver connections if http/2 requests from multiple clients share the same backend connection. An API server on a private network may choose not to enable the kube-apiserver mitigation to prevent performance regressions for unauthenticated clients. Authenticated requests rely on the fix in golang.org/x/net v0.17.0 alone. https://issue.k8s.io/121197 tracks further mitigation of http/2 attacks by authenticated clients.
